rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · The Scarecrow Comes to Jinxland
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a tiny scarecrow the size of a toy soldier standing bravely on a dark wooden table, a bent witch in patched purple robes holding up a small black bottle, a little girl in a plaid dress and a bearded old sailor glaring at her, warm candlelight in a smoky hut, gently dramatic storybook illustration

blocks.text: The tall figure stepped down off the rope bridge and into Jinxland. It was the Scarecrow of Oz himself, straw hat, patched coat and all. "I heard there was trouble in this valley," he said pleasantly, "so I came as fast as walking would carry me. And I must say, trouble is my favorite kind of visitor." Trot decided at once that she liked him.

Blinkie the witch was watching from her hut on the hill, and she did not like wise strangers one bit. She fetched a little black bottle, muttered three words backwards, and shook it hard over the valley. Then she chuckled, which is a wicked sort of laugh. Quick as a wink, the Scarecrow shrank down, down, down. Soon he stood no taller than a toy soldier on a shelf.
Blinkie's bottle shrinks the Scarecrow small as a toy.

But Trot and Cap'n Bill were not afraid of any witch, big or little. They marched up the hill together and caught Blinkie by her ragged sleeves before she could sip her supper. The old witch's shoulders were thin as broomsticks, but her temper was heavy. "Make him big again," said Trot, "or you will stay caught right here all week." Blinkie believed her at once, and began to mutter.
Ask your child: Trot is the smallest one on the hill, yet Blinkie is the one who feels small. What does Trot win with — her size, or her steady voice?

Up grew the Scarecrow, tall and comfortable again. He set his hat straight and bowed to Trot. "Small, medium or large, I am the same fellow inside," he said. "Kindness does not come in sizes. Now then — a frozen heart, a wicked king, and a frightened valley. Good. I do my best work in tangles like this one."

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · Googly-Goo's Gold
chapters.artPrompt: a plump rich old man in jewelled clothes pouring gold coins from a chest before a sour-faced king on a crooked wooden throne, a torch-holding guard watching in a dim palace hall, coins gleaming in the torchlight, gently comic storybook illustration

blocks.text: Now you must hear about Googly-Goo, the richest man in Jinxland. He had gold rings on his fingers, gold chains on his waistcoat, and a heart as dry as an old biscuit. He had decided to marry Princess Gloria. Not because he loved her, but because she was lovely, and he liked owning lovely things. Nobody had ever asked Gloria what she thought.

Googly-Goo poured a whole chest of gold at King Krewl's feet. "Make the girl say yes," he said, "and every coin is yours." King Krewl looked at the gold, and his crooked mouth grew crooked with joy. "Leave it to me," said the king, which was a very silly thing to say. Kings often say silly things when gold is jingling.
Googly-Goo pours his gold at the king's crooked throne.

But there was a problem, and it was a funny one. Gloria's heart was frozen, so she could not love Googly-Goo at all. She could not love anybody — not even a rich old man with gold rings on every finger. The witch's spell had spoiled the king's plan completely, and Krewl stamped with rage when he understood. Trot heard the whole story from Pon, and her cheeks burned for Gloria.
Ask your child: Krewl wants Gloria to love Googly-Goo. Can anybody order a heart to love on command? Why not?

Pon heard the whole plan from behind the palace wall, where he had gone to look at Gloria's window. He walked straight to the gate and said, "Gloria shall not marry either of you." The guards pushed him out into the road, and the gate boomed shut behind him like a thunderclap. "Very well," said the Scarecrow calmly. "Then we shall visit the king ourselves — politely, and at the right moment."

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · The Witch's Hut
chapters.artPrompt: a bent witch in patched purple robes trembling beside a bubbling cauldron in a smoky hut, a tall scarecrow sitting calmly on a stool, a small girl in plaid and an old sailor at the low doorway, green candlelight and drifting steam, gently spooky but friendly storybook illustration

blocks.text: "The heart must be thawed," said the Scarecrow next morning, "and only one person in Jinxland knows how. So today we shall pay a call on the witch." Trot shivered, and Cap'n Bill squared his shoulders. "Can we trust her trickiness?" asked Trot. "Trust a witch? No," said the Scarecrow. "Watch her? Yes." "I've sailed through storms," said Cap'n Bill. "I suppose a hut is a kind of storm with a roof."

They climbed the hill to Blinkie's hut, the Scarecrow leading, Trot and Cap'n Bill close behind. The hill smelled of burned soup and old spiders, and the grass grew in crooked tufts. The crooked door creaked open before anybody knocked, and a thin voice floated out like smoke. "Go away, all of you! I am busy, and I am cross, and I know why you have come."
Blinkie trembles in her smoky hut.

But the Scarecrow only stepped inside and sat down, calm as Sunday. "What a curious smell your pot has," he said politely. "I hear that Glinda, the good sorceress of Oz, keeps a list of naughty witches. Hers is a very long list, and she never loses it." Blinkie went whiter than milk. Trot had never seen anybody look so scared of a stuffed man.
New word: thaw — to melt something frozen, slow and gently. Freezing Gloria's heart took Blinkie one minute; thawing it will need real work.

"D-don't send for Glinda!" the witch stammered. "I'll do anything." "Good," said the Scarecrow, standing up. "Tonight you will thaw the princess's heart, and you will do it kindly. And afterwards you will leave this valley alone for ever." Blinkie nodded so fast that her hat fell off. She began to stir a new potion at once.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Heart Thaws
chapters.artPrompt: a princess with pale golden hair waking from stillness in a candlelit room, sparkling frost melting from her hands into tiny drops, a boy gardener, a small girl in plaid and an old sailor watching with hope, warm golden light breaking through cold blue shadows, tender fairytale illustration

blocks.text: That night Blinkie crept up to the palace with a steaming pot, muttering to herself. Krewl was away in the treasury, counting Googly-Goo's gold by candlelight, so nobody stopped her. Gloria sat alone in her room, still and cold and beautiful, like a statue that had once been a girl. The moon watched from the window, and Trot watched from the doorway, and Pon watched from the shadow of the curtain.

Blinkie waved the sweet steam all around her, muttering her words backwards, and everyone held their breath. Nobody dared to cough, not even the witch. The pot bubbled like a small green sea. For a long moment nothing happened at all. Then a tiny drop of frost rolled off Gloria's hand and fell. The room felt warmer by one degree, and then by two, and then by springtime.
Frost melts away, and Gloria smiles again.

Gloria blinked. She looked around the room, and then she saw Pon, and her whole face lit up like morning. "Pon!" she cried. "Have you been here all this time?" "Yes, every single day," said Trot gently, "and we brought help." Pon took her hand and found he could not say a word. For a gardener, that is quite a thing.
Ask your child: what really thawed Gloria's heart — the witch's potion, or the friends who refused to give up? Talk about which one you would call the magic.

Trot wiped her eyes and laughed at the same time. Only Blinkie slipped out through the door, grumbling into the dark. "The king will be angry when he hears," whispered Cap'n Bill. And far away in his gold room, King Krewl heard the very first rumor, and began to shout. "Then we had better be quick," said the Scarecrow, "for I have a fountain to show him."

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The Forbidden Fountain
chapters.artPrompt: a tall scarecrow with a big watering can hiding behind a marble fountain in a moonlit garden, moonlight silvering the spray of water, rose bushes and dark tidy hedges around, a quiet waiting mood, soft silvery storybook illustration

blocks.text: Krewl came storming back to the palace with all his soldiers. "Arrest them! Lock them up!" he roared. "Where is the Scarecrow?" he bellowed, which was exactly the right question. But the Scarecrow had spent the afternoon being busy and quiet, which is his favorite way of being clever. He had found a garden with a fountain in it, and the fountain was very special indeed.

It was the Forbidden Fountain, and no one in Jinxland was allowed to drink from it. Only the gardener knew, and he never told. The water was clear and cool and looked like ordinary water. But anyone who drank it forgot everything they knew. Their name, their plans, their naughtiness — all of it, washed away clean as a plate.
The Scarecrow waits with a watering can by the Forbidden Fountain.

The Scarecrow borrowed the gardener's biggest watering can and filled it quietly. Then he waited in the roses, patient as Sunday. Sure enough, King Krewl came stomping through the garden after his enemies, shouting at the moon. The Scarecrow stepped out, tipped the can, and splash — the furious king was covered from crown to boots. Water dripped off the king's mustache like small silver ropes. "Now, now," said the Scarecrow soothingly. "You were shouting a moment ago. Isn't that tiring?"
Talk about it: the magic water does not hurt Krewl. It only washes his pride and naughtiness away. Is forgetting sometimes a kindness?

Krewl blinked at the fountain like a little boy lost at a party. "Who am I?" he asked. "And why is everybody looking at me?" Nobody felt cross with him now, because there was nothing left to be cross about. The soldiers put down their spears, and one of them began to laugh. Somewhere a nightingale started up, as if it approved.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · A King for Jinxland
chapters.artPrompt: a gentle young gardener crowned with a simple green wreath in a sunny palace square, a golden-haired princess smiling beside him, a crowd of happy country folk waving straw hats, a scarecrow, a small girl and an old sailor on the palace steps, bright festive light, joyful storybook illustration

blocks.text: By morning, all Jinxland knew that the wicked king had been washed like a dish. The people came running from every cornfield and cabbage patch to the palace square. Without a king, the land would be muddled, so the Scarecrow stood up on the palace steps and called for quiet. Trot sat on the steps with her chin in her hands, thinking how strange and fine it all was.

"Who shall rule you now?" he asked. The people looked at each other. Then everybody looked at Pon, and Pon looked at his boots, and went as red as a poppy. The Scarecrow had to wave both arms before anybody could hear the next thing. "Pon! Pon! Pon!" shouted the whole square, until the cornfields shook on the far side of the valley.
The people cheer for their new king, Pon.

So Pon the gardener became King Pon, with Gloria beaming beside him, and Jinxland cheered till dinner time. Googly-Goo slunk home to count his rings and was heard from no more. As for old Krewl, the water had washed his cruelty away with his crown. He asked, very politely, for a garden spade. The people gave him the sunniest patch by the wall.
Ask your child: the people chose Pon because he was kind. Make a list together of three kind things a good ruler could do this week.

He dug and planted all that summer, happier than he had ever been as a king. "Jinxland is mended," said the Scarecrow at last, dusting off his hat. "And now, my friends, I think it is time somebody grander met you. Have you ever heard of a city made of emeralds, where the gates shine green and nobody is ever unkind?" Trot and Cap'n Bill looked at each other, and their eyes grew wide.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · Over the Gulf
chapters.artPrompt: a round friendly bird with a spinning fan-shaped tail flying through soft morning mist over an enormous deep gulf, a little girl in plaid clinging happily to his back, the far green rim of Jinxland glowing behind, airy bright storybook illustration

blocks.text: The way back to Oz lay across the great gulf. The gulf is too wide to walk and too deep to dream about. But the Ork came whirring back that very morning, spinning his fan tail with pride. "One more flight," he said. "Then I really must find my own country, you know." "Small wings, big heart," said Cap'n Bill, which is the finest thing a sailor can say about anybody.

He carried Trot first, then Cap'n Bill, then the Scarecrow, out over the mist. Below them the gulf yawned, deep and blue and quiet as a sleeping whale. Trot held on with her knees and her fingers and her hopes. The Ork sang a flying song, mostly made of honks, and kept his round wings steady as a table. Trot laughed into the wind and did not feel one bit afraid, which surprised her very much.
The Ork flies the friends home across the great gulf.

On the far side they waved goodbye to Jinxland, where Gloria and King Pon stood waving back from the corn. Then the road turned toward the Emerald City, and the Scarecrow walked between his new friends, telling them about Oz. Trot asked a hundred questions, and the Scarecrow answered them all, even the ones without answers. "Ozma will love you," he said. "She collects interesting people, and you are both very interesting."
New word: gulf — you met this word way back in Chapter 2. Can you remember what it means? Retell how the friends first crossed it.

They walked through meadows and chattering brooks and little villages, and each day the world looked greener. Then one morning the sky itself turned gently green — and there stood the shining walls of the Emerald City. "Well, I never," said Cap'n Bill, taking off his hat.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · The Emerald City
chapters.artPrompt: a graceful girl-queen in a green gown greeting a small girl in plaid and a bearded old sailor in a glittering emerald throne room, a scarecrow bowing happily, Dorothy waving by a tall window, green marble columns and soft chandeliers, warm welcoming light, grand but cozy storybook illustration

blocks.text: Ozma of Oz was waiting at the palace doors, and the whole city seemed to be waiting with her. "Welcome, Trot. Welcome, Cap'n Bill," she said, as if she had known them for years. "The Scarecrow wrote to me about you. Well — he talked to me about you, and I listened through magic, which is even better." Green marble shone everywhere, even on the flowerpots, and Trot kept forgetting to close her mouth.

Dorothy ran up and took Trot's hand at once, and the two girls were friends before the first cup of tea was poured. Cap'n Bill told the whole story that evening, whirlpool and all. Even the palace cook left the soup to listen. The Scarecrow added all the best parts about himself, which made everybody laugh until the candlesticks wobbled.
Ozma welcomes Trot and Cap'n Bill to the Emerald City.

"You have both been very brave," said Ozma at last. "Will you stay and live here in Oz?" Trot looked at Cap'n Bill. Cap'n Bill looked at Trot. Then they said yes together, so quickly that they bumped heads, and everybody laughed again, and Ozma clapped her hands with joy. "Then it is settled," she said, "and I am very glad."
Ask your child: the story began with a whirlpool and ends with a welcome. What changed for Trot and Cap'n Bill? What stayed the same all along?

So the little girl and the old sailor found a home at last, with no more whirlpools unless they asked for one nicely. And far away in Jinxland, the corn grew tall and the king dug his garden. A frozen heart became just a story to tell on winter nights. And on quiet evenings, Trot and Dorothy compared adventure stories, and neither one ever told the biggest one.
